title: We laugh far more with others
hook: People laugh around 30 times more often with company than when alone.
peek: Laughter feels like a reaction to jokes, but studies by the neuroscientist Robert Provine found it is mostly a social signal. People laugh far more with others than alone, and most laughter follows ordinary remarks rather than punchlines.
lede: We tend to think we laugh because something is funny. The neuroscientist Robert Provine, at the University of Maryland, spent years listening to real laughter in everyday life and found a different picture. Laughter is mainly about other people. It is a signal we send to each other, and jokes have surprisingly little to do with most of it.

bullets.text: In a 1989 study, Provine and a colleague asked students to note every time they laughed for a week. They laughed about 30 times more often when they were with other people than when they were alone.

Provine's team logged about 1,200 bursts of laughter overheard in shopping centres and on campuses. Only around 10 to 20% followed anything resembling a joke. Most came after ordinary remarks such as see you later or I know.
In those conversations, the person speaking laughed more than the person listening. That suggests laughter often works less as a response to humour and more as a friendly signal from the speaker.
Laughter almost never interrupts a phrase. People laugh at the pauses, at the end of a sentence or between them, much like punctuation in writing. Provine called this the punctuation effect.
